title: Guidelines for Developing New Teacher Mentoring Programs (NTMPs)
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Written after his district asked him to think about new teacher mentoring, this rough-draft essay proposes a single guiding 'Everest statement': these programs exist to engage and develop new teachers until they become credible, long-term educators. Dave Stuart Jr. then unpacks each term. Engagement means cultivating the five key beliefs (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy), which research shows are malleable, contextual and predictive, and he argues motivation should be chosen first over development. Development means memorizing a small number of 'sets of knowns' (an idea borrowed from Montana educator Tammy Elser) and demonstrating a short list of core competencies, set by small expert committees who keep less as more. Credibility is defined through care, competence, passion and repair, and long-term retention is the final aim given the cost of turnover. The piece reads as a design brief for anyone running or informally supporting new-teacher mentoring.
points: A mentoring program needs one memorable Everest statement that every stakeholder can use to test decisions.
Engagement comes before development: a motivated new teacher will find a way to fix weaknesses, while an overwhelmed one disengages.
Teacher evaluation frameworks are too sprawling to guide development, so programs should cohere around a precious few knowledge sets and competencies.
Expert committees should build 'sets of knowns' (motivation, classroom management, lesson templates, core strategies, local knowledge) because skill cannot precede knowledge.
Credibility, defined as care, competence, passion and repair, is the exit standard, and retention is justified by the high cost of turnover.
quotes: Low-touch, high-leverage interventions that work well in belief cultivation for students are likely to work well in new teacher engagement. So just as the Belonging belief is efficiently cultivated in students through teacher-generated moments of genuine connection, mentor-generated moments of genuine connection will produce a similar result.

Motivation is the first ingredient because a well-motivated teacher will find a way to develop him- or herself in areas of weakness. If you have to pick between engagement and development, pick engagement.

Effective teams and people cohere their efforts around a precious few things, not the exhaustive many. Frameworks like those mandated for teacher evaluation in the state of Michigan exemplify the exhaustive many versus the precious few.

Montana educator Tammy Elser requires her undergraduate teacher preparation students to master “sets of knowns” — a packet of items and lists and diagrams that her students are expected to memorize and explain during a semester with her. This sounds criminally arcane to most twenty-first-century educational thinkers, but it is fundamentally brilliant.
Teacher turnover is expensive in fiscal, human, and emotional capital. It is also expensive in terms of the school’s reputation, as new teachers inevitably take time to get their feet under them.
